content.title: Classes Connect Structure and Presentation
content.hook: You already know CSS can describe how an element should look. Now the browser lets JavaScript decide which existing class an element should have.
content.context: You already know CSS can describe how an element should look. Now the browser lets JavaScript decide which existing class an element should have.
goals: Use `classList` to add, remove, and toggle classes so JavaScript can change presentation through existing CSS rules.

content.title: The connection
content.text:
Suppose the page already contains a CSS rule for `.active` and an element: ```html

Offline

``` JavaScript can add the class: ```js const status = document.querySelector("#status"); status.classList.add("active"); ``` It can remove it: ```js status.classList.remove("active"); ``` Or toggle it: ```js status.classList.toggle("active"); ``` You are not rewriting the CSS rule. You are changing which classes the element currently has.

content.question:
If an element already has `class="card"` and this runs:

```js
card.classList.add("selected");
```

what is the likely new class list?

content.title: Try it
content.text:
Use this starting point: ```html

Offline

``` Add and remove a class called `active`. ```js const status = document.querySelector("#status"); status.classList.add("active"); status.classList.remove("active"); ``` Then try: ```js status.classList.toggle("active"); ``` Observe that `toggle` flips the class between present and absent.

content.title: Why this pattern matters
content.text:
Separating responsibilities makes code easier to reason about:

- CSS defines what the `active` state looks like.
- JavaScript decides when the `active` state applies.

That means behavior can change without rewriting the visual rule each time.
